query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is governed by the formation of nanoscale crystalline/amorphous (C/A) and amorphous/amorphous (A/A) interfacial structures, which suppress shear banding instability and promote homogeneous deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings with nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures
generation.intervention: Introduction of ductile crystalline phases or nanoscale A/A interfaces through engineering of MG-based composites or development of amorphous alloys
generation.conditions: Nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures, high density of interfaces, and controlled composition and processing conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures, shear transformation zones (STZs), and crystalline phases
generation.mechanism: Suppression of shear banding instability, promotion of homogeneous deformation, and enhancement of plasticity through the formation of nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation, increased tensile strength and ductility, and enhanced mechanical properties
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloys without nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures
generation.boundary: Limited by the composition, processing conditions, and interface density, which can affect the formation and stability of nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanisms by which nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures suppress shear banding instability and promote homogeneous deformation are not fully understood and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of the mechanical properties of high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings with and without nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of nanoscale C/A and A/A interfacial structures does not lead to improved resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation and enhanced mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

By adjusting the atomic ratios of metals, adding interstitial atoms, and improving manufacturing processes, HEA with outstanding mechanical properties, high-temperature performance, corrosion resistance, and wear resistance can be designed to accommodate the requirements of specific working environments. HEAs have attracted the attention of numerous researchers due to their excellent comprehensive performance and have quickly become a research hotspot. CoCrFeMnNi HEA is a single-phase high entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, first proposed by Cantor and his colleagues. This alloy, characterized by high mixing entropy, large lattice distortion, and slow diffusion rates due to similar atomic ratios, is widely studied in the field of metallic materials.
CoCrFeMnNi HEA has low stacking fault energy and can activate both dislocation slip and deformation twinning (DT) mechanisms simultaneously. Additionally, It may undergo hexagonal closed-packed (HCP) phase transformation under low temperature, high pressure, high strain rate, and severe plastic deformation environments. The synergistic effect of multiple deformation mechanisms gives it good plastic deformation abi

the starting point for further modifications of the chemical composition aimed at improving specific performance parameters. Often, the CoCrFeNi alloy is modified by the addition of alloying elements such as Nb, Ti, W, or Zr [,,]; however, recently, there has been a growing interest in the field of HEAs with vanadium (V), which is considered unique among alloying elements [,,,,,,]. The uniqueness of V is manifested in its atomic volume, which is large in FCC-structured alloys and small in the case of the alloys with a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. This leads to a significant volume mismatch in both crystal structures, resulting in strong strengthening effects in both FCC and BCC HEAs []. Significant strengthening combined with a loss of ductility in V-containing alloys has also been demonstrated as a result of the formation of the sigma (σ) phase [], the amount of which is directly related to the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of HEA.
